images.prompt: Create ONE publication-quality realistic technical illustration for a manufacturing knowledge article, landscape 3:2 aspect ratio. Subject: SUBTRACTIVE CNC POCKET MILLING. A shallow rectangular open pocket has been milled into the billet's top face, with four naturally rounded internal corners, vertical walls and a continuous solid flat floor. One vertical solid-carbide flat-ended four-flute end mill, held concentrically in a realistic cylindrical tool holder entering from the top, is currently side-cutting the inside right wall of this pocket: bottom cutting end at pocket floor, flute side touching stock wall, no disconnected tool, no intersecting holder. Tool holder safely above top face, short stiff tool projection. A few physically plausible short curled aluminum chips near the contact show material removal, no sparks. Keep pocket large and simple, wide access around cutter, no thin walls, no holes, no extra protrusions. Orthographically coherent isometric engineering visualization with restrained photorealistic metal materials and crisp edges; white/light neutral studio background and soft contact shadows. Billet, jaws, holder and cutting interface dominate frame, all essential workholding visible; crop only upper spindle extension. This must clearly teach removal of material from a larger block, not deposition. No people, no machine brands, no logos, no arrows, no numbers, no text, no dimensions, no decorative graphics, no border. This is an explanatory illustration, not a poster. Render exact mechanically plausible geometry and inspect tool-to-work contact carefully.

images.prompt: Create ONE publication-quality realistic technical illustration for a manufacturing knowledge article, landscape 3:2 aspect ratio, matching a clean isometric studio engineering render. Subject: FDM MATERIAL-EXTRUSION 3D PRINTING. Close oblique three-quarter view of a simple partially printed hollow rectangular blue polymer tray on a flat dark-gray build plate. Clearly visible fine parallel horizontal layer lines on all outer and inner vertical walls; flat solid bottom bonded to plate, open top, rounded rectangular corners. The current top layer has a visibly continuous narrow deposited bead tracing the wall perimeter. Above the near-right top corner, ONE mechanically plausible small brass conical nozzle pointing vertically downward from a compact metal heater block, its tip just contacting the newly deposited bead at top wall level, no large air gap, no detached plastic drops, no nozzle buried in plastic. Show enough of a conventional hot end and finned heat break above the heater block to identify extrusion but do not clutter with a complete machine. The wall supports every fresh bead underneath; do not show extrusion into midair, flying strands or large unsupported bridges. Show only modest rounded extrusion-road texture, not laminated slabs, threads or a wireframe. The actual tray is blue, build plate and printhead are neutral metal with brass nozzle, white/light neutral studio background with soft contact shadows. Tray fills most lower frame; close enough to understand material added layer by layer. All geometry perspective coherent, nozzle vertical perpendicular to build plate, tray resting flat on plate. Do not imply FDM is all additive manufacturing; this is specifically filament extrusion. No people, no branding, no logos, no text, no numbers, no arrows, no captions, no dimensions, no border, no inset diagrams. Elegant realistic engineering visualization rather than an abstract icon.
images.review: Tray rests on plate; horizontal layers remain continuous; brass nozzle meets the top wall bead. Caption identifies FDM specifically rather than generalizing this nozzle to resin or powder processes.

images.prompt: Create ONE publication-quality realistic technical illustration of PRESS-BRAKE AIR BENDING for a manufacturing knowledge article, landscape 3:2. The entire illustration must be mechanically correct. Close oblique front three-quarter view along the end of real press-brake tooling, so the V-shaped cross section and contact points are unmistakable. One straight narrow steel upper punch descends vertically from above. Its lower tip is a rounded acute wedge aligned exactly over the center of the lower V-die groove. One thin blue sheet metal strip lies BETWEEN the punch and lower die, currently partially bent into a wide shallow V by the descending punch. Sheet has perfectly constant thickness and smoothly rounded inside bend, not a sharp zero-radius corner. Punch tip contacts the blue sheet at its middle; left and right wings rise outward and rest on the two rounded upper shoulders of the lower V die. There must be clearly visible AIR GAPS between each sloping sheet wing and the sloping walls of the V groove; this is three-point AIR BENDING, not bottoming. Sheet stays visibly above the very bottom of the groove and wraps smoothly below the punch tip without tool intersections. Blue sheet is one continuous piece extending equally left/right beyond the die shoulders. Long punch edge, bend line and die groove run along the same straight longitudinal axis in consistent perspective. Show the near end cross section of the V die clearly and enough length of tooling behind it to understand the setup, all extrusions parallel. Lower die is a solid neutral-steel rectangular block with a continuous symmetrical V groove on its top. No impossible scissors, no L bracket, no folding animation, no ghosted before/after outlines, no detached sheet, no chips or material removal. Restrained photorealistic studio engineering render on white/light neutral background with soft shadows; blue only identifies the deforming sheet, tooling neutral steel. Large clear open space around contact for legibility. No people, no logos or branding, no text, numbers, arrows, labels, diagrams, borders, or dimensions. This image teaches bending changes sheet shape while retaining its material.
images.review: Continuous blue sheet contacts the punch and both die shoulders; rounded bend and air clearance remain above the V walls and bottom. No drawn fold arrow or detached sheet is used.

limits: Teaching illustrations, not equipment photographs, validated machine setups, dimensioned manufacturing instructions or measured results.
